title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova

blocks.html: Until BERT, the standard recipe for pre-trained language models was left-to-right autoregressive modeling: predict the next token given the previous ones (GPT-1, ELMo's LM half). That works for generation, but every representation a token gets only sees the words to its left.

For understanding tasks — question answering, classification, named entity recognition — the right context matters as much as the left. ELMo concatenates a left-to-right and a right-to-left LM, but that's two separate models stitched together, not jointly bidirectional.

BERT pre-trains a single deep Transformer encoder bidirectionally using a clever objective (Masked Language Modeling, below). At fine-tune time, you add a small task-specific head on top of BERT and train the whole thing on your downstream task.

BERT advances the state of the art for eleven NLP tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), and SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2.
BERT is a stack of Transformer encoder layers — no decoder, no autoregression. Two sizes were released:

Input format: a single sequence that can encode either one sentence or a pair. Tokens are WordPiece sub-words. Special tokens: [CLS] at the start (its final hidden state is the pooled representation), [SEP] between segments.
Input embedding = token embedding + segment embedding (which sentence?) + position embedding (learned, not sinusoidal).

Randomly mask 15% of input tokens; train the model to predict the original. Bidirectional context flows naturally because every token attends to every other (subject to the mask) — but the model can't trivially solve the task by copying its input.
Subtlety: at fine-tune time there are no [MASK] tokens, which would create a train/test mismatch. BERT handles this by varying what 'mask' means:

items: 80% of selected tokens are replaced with [MASK].
10% are replaced with a random vocabulary token.

blocks.html: The model has to predict the original token at every selected position — but it doesn't know which positions were perturbed, so it has to maintain a distributional representation everywhere.

Many downstream tasks (QA, NLI) require modeling the relationship between two sentences. BERT pre-trains for this by adding a binary classification task: given two sentences A and B, is B the actual next sentence after A (50% of the time) or a random other sentence (50%)? Prediction is made from the final [CLS] representation.
Later work (RoBERTa, ALBERT) found NSP contributes little to downstream quality — the data variety it provides matters more than the specific objective. BERT's success comes overwhelmingly from MLM.

For every downstream task: take pre-trained BERT, attach a small task head (a single linear layer for classification; a span-extraction head for SQuAD; etc.), train end-to-end with a small learning rate ($\sim 2$–$5 \times 10^{-5}$) for 2–4 epochs. The whole model is updated.
No task-specific architectural choices. The same BERT plus a different last layer covers sentence classification, sentence-pair tasks, span prediction (QA), and token-level tagging (NER).
BERT-Large set state-of-the-art on 11 NLP tasks at release. Highlights:

items: GLUE (8 NLU tasks averaged): 80.5%, +7.7 over prior SOTA.

blocks.html: The size of the jumps over prior state-of-the-art was unusual — most papers improve numbers by tenths of a point. BERT's gains were 3-5% absolute, sometimes more. NLP collectively reset.

Before BERT: NLP was a constellation of task-specific architectures, each starting from scratch (sometimes with word embeddings). After BERT: everyone uses pre-trained Transformer encoders. The recipe of 'huge model + masked self-supervised pre-training + cheap task-specific fine-tuning' became the field's default.

Direct descendants: RoBERTa (BERT with better training), ALBERT (parameter sharing), DistilBERT (compression), ELECTRA (replaced-token-detection instead of MLM), DeBERTa (disentangled attention), and the entire encoder-only branch of modern NLP. T5 generalized it to encoder-decoder; modern LLMs (GPT-3+, Claude, Gemini) followed the autoregressive path BERT explicitly didn't take. Both branches inherit the 'pre-train at scale, fine-tune cheaply' template BERT established.
